strengths: The paper presents a clean and well-motivated framework (CG-BGs) that combines the scalability of coarse-grained generative surrogates with the statistical rigor of importance reweighting from Boltzmann Generators, addressing a genuine limitation of CG Boltzmann Emulators (persistent bias without reweighting).

The use of enhanced-sampling force matching (ESFM) to learn the PMF target energy from rapidly converged biased data is a practical and well-grounded choice, with Propositions 2-3 (from Chen et al., 2026) correctly establishing why fiber-distribution invariance permits biased-data training.

Experiments are carefully controlled: explicit solvent is used as reference rather than implicit solvent, two CG resolutions are compared, flows trained on biased vs. unbiased data are compared, and the framework is repurposed as a simulation-free diagnostic for evaluating learned PMFs (PMF_U vs. PMF_B), which is a genuinely useful secondary contribution.

Reproducibility is strong: datasets, architectures, training hyperparameters, simulation protocols (GROMACS/PLUMED, mdrun -rerun for unbiased force labels), compute costs, and public code are all provided.

The limitations discussion is honest (predefined CVs, resolution degeneracy, and the analysis in G.2 of the bias introduced by weight clipping), and the weight-clipping ablation transparently shows that unclipped reweighting fails (near-zero ESS), exposing a real practical issue rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is largely compositional: CFM-based flows in CG space, ESFM-learned PMFs, and importance reweighting are all existing components, and the theory (Props. 1-3) is either standard (LSI + Fisher divergence argument, proved in A.1) or directly from prior work. The main novelty is the combination and the demonstration.

The central scalability claim is not directly demonstrated: experiments are limited to the 2D Müller-Brown potential and alanine dipeptide (6-10 beads, ~22 solute atoms). The abstract and conclusion frame CG-BGs as a 'scalable pathway for unbiased sampling of larger molecular systems,' but no larger or more complex system is tested, so this claim remains speculative.

The 'asymptotically exact / unbiased' framing is overstated given the method as implemented: (i) weight clipping is required for stable results (0% clipping yields near-zero ESS), which introduces bias that the authors themselves quantify but treat as a settled trade-off; (ii) the target energy is a learned PMF U_eta, so reweighting is only as unbiased as the PMF approximation on the support of q_theta (acknowledged in Sec. 3.3 but in tension with stronger claims elsewhere). Reported ESS values (~0.19-0.25) are modest.

The theoretical bound in Proposition 1 relies on a global LSI, which the authors admit is unrealistic for multimodal PMFs; the bound is presented as motivation but provides little practical assurance for the multimodal systems of interest.

The contribution to PMF learning itself is limited: PMF_U (learned from long unbiased MD) actually performs worse than PMF_B in their own benchmark, echoing prior findings (Chen et al., 2026; Görlich & Zavadlav, 2025), so the paper mainly confirms known behavior rather than resolving PMF-learning difficulties.

Comparison baselines are somewhat limited: implicit-solvnet GB models and an all-atom CFM cost comparison, but no direct head-to-head against other CG samplers with reweighting (e.g., prior BG variants with CG mappings) on identical data, and quantitative evaluation is restricted to dihedral-based metrics (JS, PMF error, ESS) for a single small molecule.

strengths: The paper is well written and clearly structured: the CG-BG workflow (Sec. 3, Fig. 1) and the relationship between BGs, Boltzmann Emulators, and force matching are explained accessibly.

The core idea is sensible and addresses a real gap: Boltzmann Emulators lack reweighting, and atomistic BGs do not scale; combining an ML potential of mean force with a flow proposal and importance weights is a principled way to restore asymptotic correctness in CG space.

The simulation-free benchmarking of learned PMFs (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 5) is a genuinely useful practical contribution — one-shot evaluation of candidate PMFs against the PMF-defined Boltzmann distribution without further MD is a nice diagnostic tool.

Reproducibility of the experimental setup is above average: simulation details (Table 3), architectures, hyperparameters, algorithms (§F), compute hardware, and a weight-clipping ablation (Table 6, Fig. 12) are all provided, and the bias–variance trade-off of clipping is discussed honestly.
The authors honestly flag key limitations: reliance on predefined CVs, degradation at coarser mappings, and that weight clipping sacrifices strict unbiasedness.
weaknesses: The central claim of scalability is not supported by the evidence. The only molecular system evaluated is alanine dipeptide (a 22-atom textbook benchmark) plus the Müller–Brown toy potential. The abstract and conclusion assert 'a scalable pathway for the unbiased sampling of larger molecular systems,' but no larger system (e.g., a peptide with metastable structure or a protein) is tested. This is the paper's headline claim and it is unvalidated.

Limited novelty. The method is essentially a composition of existing components: continuous normalizing flows trained by CFM (Lipman et al., Tong et al.), variational force matching (Noid et al., 2008), enhanced-sampling force matching with the fiber-distribution invariance result (Chen et al., 2026 — Propositions 2 and 3 are explicitly attributed to that paper), and weight clipping from prior BG work (Tan et al., 2025a; Gloy & Olsson, 2025). Proposition 1 is a standard LSI/Fisher-divergence bound whose assumption (global LSI for multimodal PMFs) the authors themselves note is unrealistic. The claimed 'first BG formulation with MLP target energies' is a thin novelty claim and likely contestable.

Exactness is overstated. The reweighting is only exact with respect to the learned PMF Uη, not the true marginal p(R); any force-matching error propagates into the 'exact' equilibrium statistics. Moreover, the 1% weight clipping used in all headline results (Table 2) introduces bias, as the authors' own ablation shows (Fig. 12: aggressive clipping increases bias). Table 2 results should therefore be described as biased estimates, yet they are presented as recovering 'unbiased equilibrium statistics.'

The reported advantage over 'implicit solvent MD baselines' is a weak and somewhat misleading comparison. CG-BGs win over GB models essentially because they are trained on explicit-solvent data — the comparison says more about the solvent model than about the generative method. There is no comparison against a natural alternative such as running enhanced sampling plus reweighting directly, or against a CG Boltzmann Emulator with reweighting.

There is an implicit circularity the paper does not confront: the flow proposal is trained on the same (biased) data from which the PMF is learned, so the reweighted result largely reflects the quality of the PMF; the flow contributes little beyond a proposal density, and the paper does not isolate or quantify its benefit relative to simply reweighting the biased dataset itself.

Residual discrepancies from the MD reference remain visible in several results (e.g., the ψ free-energy profiles in Fig. 13, and Core Beta profiles in Fig. 4c–d), yet the text characterizes agreement as 'close' without quantifying when the method's error becomes acceptable.

The footnote claiming public code ('Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/') is incomplete in the manuscript — no actual repository URL is given — which undermines the reproducibility claim as submitted.

The experimental scope is small relative to the framing: with only two low-dimensional systems, metrics like ESS (~0.2–0.25) and JS divergence are reported without error analysis over seeds beyond ±std, and there is no stress test of the method in the regime where BGs are claimed to fail (larger systems, poor overlap).

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized; the CG-BG workflow (PMF learning via ESFM + flow-matching proposal + importance reweighting) is presented coherently with a good balance of background and new material.

The framework is principled: reweighting in CG space against a learned PMF restores thermodynamic consistency that CG Boltzmann Emulators lack, and using ESFM (Chen et al., 2026) means the PMF target can be learned from rapidly converged biased data rather than long unbiased trajectories, which is a practical advantage.

The experiments are careful and thorough for the systems studied: Müller–Brown (with an analytically exact reference) and alanine dipeptide in explicit solvent, with two CG mappings, biased and unbiased training data, quantitative metrics (JS divergence, PMF error, ESS), an honest ablation of weight clipping (Tab. 6, Fig. 12) showing the bias-variance tradeoff, and timing comparisons against prior atomistic BG methods (Tab. 4).

Section 4.3 (simulation-free benchmarking of learned PMFs) is a genuinely useful secondary contribution: reusing one set of flow samples with different PMFs to rapidly diagnose CG potentials is a nice, practical idea.

Limitations are discussed honestly (predefined CVs, degeneracy of coarser mappings, need for enhanced sampling bias potentials), and experimental detail in the appendix (simulation parameters, architectures, algorithms, compute) is strong, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central scalability claim is not demonstrated. The abstract and introduction repeatedly frame CG-BGs as a 'scalable pathway for the unbiased sampling of larger molecular systems,' but the largest system is alanine dipeptide (22 atoms, reduced to 6–10 beads). This is arguably smaller than systems addressed by recent atomistic BG work the paper itself cites (Klein & Noé, 2024; Tan et al., 2025a). The scalability argument rests entirely on reduced dimensionality rather than evidence.

Novelty is modest. The framework is a recombination of established components: force matching (Noid et al., 2008), enhanced-sampling force matching (Chen et al., 2026 — Propositions 2 and 3 are restated from that work), flow matching (Lipman et al., 2022), and self-normalized importance sampling (Noé et al., 2019). Proposition 1 is a standard Fisher-divergence/LSI bound. The claimed novelty ('first BG formulation that incorporates MLPs as the target energy') is a relatively thin delta over Chen et al. (2026) plus reweighting.

The 'asymptotically exact' framing is undermined in practice: (i) the weights are taken against the learned PMF Uη, so unbiasedness holds only relative to a PMF that itself has force-matching error; and (ii) 1% weight clipping is required to avoid catastrophic weight degeneracy (ESS ≈ 0 without it, Tab. 6), which introduces a small but systematic bias that the paper acknowledges only as a 'bias–variance trade-off.' The exactness claim should be more carefully qualified.

The claim that CG-BGs provide 'a correction mechanism for existing CG Boltzmann Emulators' is never tested directly — no experiment takes a published CG emulator and shows the proposed reweighting corrects its bias.

The comparison in Tab. 4 against prior BG training/inference costs is not apples-to-apples (different systems/architectures; results borrowed from Rehman et al., 2025 under †), and the all-atom baseline excludes solvent, which the authors themselves note would be the proper reference.

Some units and reporting are unclear: ESS values in Tab. 2 (~0.23) appear to be a fraction, but this is never stated; minor typos ('divegence', 'Jenson-Shannon'); the released-code footnote appears truncated in the manuscript (github.com/...), weakening the reproducibility claim.

Efficiency numbers are partially unflattering when read closely: the MACE PMF training time (Tab. 5) plus flow training can approach the cost saved by coarse-graining, so the end-to-end efficiency gain over the all-atom baseline (4.16h vs 0.84–1.45h total, but ignoring PMF training) deserves more careful accounting.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and technically sound: performing BG-style importance reweighting directly in coarse-grained coordinate space, using a learned PMF as the target energy, restores asymptotic correctness to CG generative surrogates (Boltzmann Emulators) that currently lack any reweighting mechanism. This fills a genuine methodological gap.

The evaluation protocol is notably more rigorous than prior BG work: explicit solvent MD is used as the ground-truth reference rather than implicit solvent, and the implicit solvent baselines (GB OBC1/OBC2) are treated as competing models. The claim that atomistic BGs reweighted with implicit solvent energies are fundamentally capped by solvent approximation error is well supported (Tab. 2, Tab. 7).

The experiments systematically demonstrate the key claim that reweighting recovers equilibrium statistics from biased (10-50-100 ns WT-MetaD) or short data, which is the practically important setting (Fig. 2, Fig. 6, Tab. 2). The simulation-free PMF benchmarking use case (§4.3) is a nice, practically useful addition.

Thorough ablations and diagnostics: weight clipping ablations with a bias-variance analysis (Tab. 7-9, Fig. 10), resolution trade-off analysis (accuracy vs. ESS vs. cost, §4.2, Tab. 1), computational cost comparisons against atomistic BG baselines (Tab. 5), and additional results (Ramachandran plots, bond lengths, ψ dihedrals). Reproducibility is good: code is released, architectures, training details, and simulation protocols are documented in detail.
Limitations are honestly discussed (predefined CVs, partial biasing of only one dihedral pair for larger peptides, PMF convergence dependence), and the impact statement is appropriate.
weaknesses: Scale limitations undermine the headline scalability claim. The largest system is a 72-atom alanine hexapeptide, still far below the 'larger molecular systems' implied by the abstract. Moreover, quality degrades with size: hexapeptide ESS is only 0.12 and the 0%-clipped variant fails catastrophically (JS 0.197, PMF error 8.0), suggesting the approach may not extend gracefully beyond these toy-to-small peptides.

Novelty is incremental. The paper assembles existing components: Boltzmann Generators (Noé et al., 2019), force matching for CG PMFs (Noid et al., 2008), and enhanced sampling force matching, whose theoretical underpinnings (Propositions 2 and 3) are imported wholesale from Chen et al. (2026). Proposition 1 is a standard LSI argument. The genuinely new element is the combination and the reweighting-with-learned-PMF workflow, which is valuable but modest for a main-track contribution.

The 'asymptotically exact' claim is compromised in practice by the 1% weight clipping, which is itself a biasing procedure. The paper frames this as a bias-variance trade-off and ablates it, but the fact that unbiased (0% clip) reweighting fails for the tripeptide and hexapeptide (Tab. 8, Tab. 9) indicates the method's correctness guarantee is not what carries the results; the fixed clipping heuristic does. A more principled treatment (e.g., diagnostics for weight degeneracy, adaptive clipping) would strengthen the contribution.

Circularity concern in the PMF evaluation: the PMF is force-matched on explicit-solvent data, and the reference is explicit-solvent MD. Superiority over implicit solvent baselines partly reflects the training data source rather than the generative framework itself. The hexapeptide PMF is learned with biasing applied to only one dihedral pair out of six, so global PMF convergence is not established, as the authors partly acknowledge.

Theoretical results have limited force: Proposition 1 assumes a global LSI, which the authors admit is unrealistic for multimodal PMFs, and the bound involves an expectation under the learned distribution, making it hard to interpret operationally. No experiments probe the bound.

Error bars in Tables 2, 7-9 are reported but the protocol (number of independent runs, seed variability, or bootstrap) is not clearly described, making it hard to judge whether small differences (e.g., Heavy Atom 0.0048 vs. Core Beta 0.0052 JS) are meaningful.

strengths: The core idea is sensible and well-motivated: performing importance sampling in coarse-grained space against a learned PMF gives CG generative models (Boltzmann Emulators) a principled correction mechanism, which existing CG surrogates lack. Framing the PMF, rather than the atomistic energy, as the reweighting target is a clean way to reconcile reweighting correctness with dimensionality reduction.

The experimental pipeline is carefully executed and documented: explicit-solvent MD as the primary reference (a fairer choice than the implicit-solvent references common in prior BG work), both unbiased and WT-MetaD training regimes, ablations of the weight-clipping threshold (Tables 7-9, Fig. 10), Ramachandran and bond-length diagnostics in the appendix, and clear algorithms for training and reweighting.

The paper is honest about several limitations: predefined CVs, the fact that convergence is only enforced along the biased CV pair, the degeneracy/variance issue for coarser mappings (Sec. 4.2), and the need for weight clipping. The 'simulation-free benchmarking' of candidate PMFs (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 5) is a genuinely useful secondary contribution.
Presentation is generally clear, with a well-structured background section and reproducibility details (architectures, hyperparameters, hardware, software) in appendices B-E.
weaknesses: Limited originality. Every component is established: BG-style reweighting (Noé et al., 2019), flows over CG/collective variables (Tamagnone et al., 2024; Kohler et al., 2023; Stupp & Koutsourelakis, 2025), MACE-based CG PMFs (Thaler et al., 2022; Charron et al., 2025), and enhanced-sampling force matching, whose theory (Propositions 2-3) is explicitly imported from Chen et al. (2026). Proposition 1 is a standard LSI/Fisher-divergence bound whose assumptions (global LSI) the authors themselves concede are violated for multimodal PMFs. The contribution is essentially a careful assembly of known pieces.

The headline claim of scalability is not supported. The largest system is alanine hexapeptide (72 atoms), far below the 'larger molecular systems' ambition of the abstract, and the comparison table (Tab. 5) acknowledges hardware/implementation confounds. Moreover, the reported cost comparison omits the expensive part of the pipeline: the method still requires 500 ns-1500 ns of explicit-solvent atomistic MD (plus biased reruns) to train the PMF and flow, so the end-to-end computational saving relative to simply running MD is unclear.

The 'asymptotically exact' framing is overstated. The method samples the learned PMF's Boltzmann distribution, not the true marginal; any PMF error propagates into the reweighted estimates and is not corrected. The theory (Prop. 1) bounds error only under conditions that do not hold here. Validation is restricted to one biased dihedral pair per system, so correctness of the global CG distribution (and of all unbiased degrees of freedom) is not established — the authors admit this in Appendix B.2 but the main text presents free-energy agreement as evidence of equilibrium accuracy.

Evidence of reweighting quality is mixed: ESS drops to 0.12 for hexapeptide, and the results depend on clipping the top 1% of weights, which the authors themselves show introduces bias. The improvement over the raw proposal is convincing, but the comparison against atomistic BGs (TarFlow/ECNF++) is somewhat unfavorable by construction, since those baselines are trained on implicit-solvent data and evaluated against explicit-solvent references. A direct comparison to a strong CG Boltzmann Emulator trained on the same explicit-solvent data (isolating the benefit of reweighting from the choice of reference) is missing.

Minor reproducibility/presentation issues: the code-availability footnote is empty ('Our code is publicly available at' with no URL), and the training sets are large (500k-1000k samples) relative to the 'rapidly converged trajectories' narrative, which should be quantified more rigorously (e.g., convergence of PMF error vs. data amount).

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and well-motivated gap: Boltzmann Generators are limited by dimensionality and lack of overlap, while coarse-grained Boltzmann Emulators lack a reweighting correction. Combining a flow proposal over CG coordinates with importance reweighting against a learned PMF is a clean and conceptually sound way to recover asymptotically correct equilibrium statistics in reduced coordinate spaces.

The methodological pipeline is clearly presented and well organized: variational force matching, enhanced sampling force matching (ESFM) for PMF learning from rapidly converged biased data, flow matching for the proposal, and importance reweighting with ESS diagnostics are each carefully described with the relevant theory restated (Props. 1-3) and proofs provided in the appendix.

The evaluation is thoughtful: explicit solvent MD is used as the reference rather than implicit solvent (an improvement over prior BG work), implicit solvent models are treated as baselines, and the results convincingly show that reweighting recovers equilibrium dihedral free energy profiles and Ramachandran distributions even when flows are trained on short biased trajectories (10 ns WT-MetaD) or umbrella sampling data.

Section 4.3 (simulation-free benchmarking of learned PMFs by reusing a single proposal across candidate potentials) is a genuinely useful and somewhat novel secondary contribution, providing a practical tool for rapid CG force field validation.

The effect of CG resolution on the accuracy/efficiency trade-off is analyzed rather than glossed over, with a plausible mechanistic explanation (fiber-distribution degeneracy increasing conditional mean force variance under coarser mappings), and the weight clipping ablation (1% vs 0%) with sensitivity analysis is transparent about a real practical issue.

Reproducibility is strong: architectures, training hyperparameters, simulation protocols (force field, thermostat, timestep, metadynamics parameters, dataset lengths), compute hardware, and software stack are all documented in detail, and the code is stated to be publicly available.

Limitations are honestly discussed (predefined collective variables, partial convergence of the PMF along only biased degrees of freedom), and the limitations discussion does not overstate what was achieved.
weaknesses: The central scalability claim ('a practical route toward equilibrium sampling of larger molecular systems') is only weakly supported: the largest system is alanine hexapeptide (72 atoms), which is still small by molecular standards. The efficiency gains over atomistic BGs (Tab. 5) are demonstrated on small systems where Jacobian cost savings are easy to obtain, and comparisons to prior work (ECNF++, SBG, FALCON) come from a different paper with different hardware and conventions, weakening the cost claims.

The theory supporting the method is largely inherited rather than new: Proposition 1 is a standard LSI-based Fisher divergence bound, and Propositions 2 and 3 are explicitly attributed to Chen et al. (2026). The genuine technical novelty is limited to combining existing components (BG reweighting, flow matching, ESFM-learned PMFs) in CG space, which is close to prior work such as Kohler et al. (2023), Tamagnone et al. (2024), and Stupp & Koutsourelakis (2025).

The PMF is learned accurately only along the biased collective variables (the authors concede convergence 'is primarily enforced along the targeted collective variables'), yet claims of 'asymptotically correct' and 'unbiased' estimation are repeated throughout. In practice, accuracy is approximate in two compounding ways: learned PMF approximation bias and weight clipping (top 1% discarded), which formally biases the estimator. The framework's guarantees are weaker than the framing suggests.

Evaluation is concentrated on a small number of observables (phi/psi dihedrals, energy histograms, bond lengths) in low-dimensional CG representations. There is no assessment of whether the learned PMFs or reweighted ensembles are accurate for observables involving degrees of freedom not targeted by the bias, which is precisely where ESFM with partial CV biasing could fail.

No direct experimental comparison against the closest related methods (e.g., Tamagnone et al. 2024 or Kohler et al. 2023) on the same systems; comparisons rely on cited numbers with acknowledged hardware/inference caveats.

The reported ESS values (e.g., 0.12-0.55) are moderate, and the improvements over raw flow proposals in JS divergence are sometimes numerically small; the practical significance of the quantitative gaps versus implicit solvent baselines, while directionally clear, would benefit from more careful statistical treatment across seeds and error bars on the free energy profiles.

For the hexapeptide, only the Core Beta mapping is evaluated (Heavy Atom rows are dashes in Tab. 3), so the claimed trade-off between resolution and accuracy is not fully verified at the largest system size.
